r: This orientation course surveys land surveying's legal, technical, and professional foundations: federal and state statutes governing practice, and the daily-practice cycle of research, data collection, and data reduction. Observed-usage data shows Computer & Mathematical work is the largest AI usage category, and models can already summarize regulatory frameworks and outline data-reduction workflows competently. But adoption among surveying programs and practitioners remains uneven, and this two-credit course functions primarily as professional orientation for entering majors rather than performance of a task an AI could substitute for. Verification burden is moderate: students must internalize statutory context accurately, not merely retrieve a summary of it. No general-studies designation applies here, but the introductory course sits inside the program's accreditation-linked sequence. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this professional orientation and grounding in surveying's legal-technical structure is not eroded; AI assists information lookup without replacing the orientation itself.

By 2031, AI tools will fluently explain surveying statutes, licensing frameworks, and the research-collection-reduction cycle, and task-exposure research classifies this kind of informational, non-physical content among categories with rising exposure. The instrumental case for dedicated classroom delivery of this material weakens: students could plausibly self-study much of the regulatory overview using an AI tutor. What holds the course in place is its structural role introducing students to the accredited surveying-technology sequence and its professional norms, a role a general-purpose AI explainer does not replace within an academic program. The rating rises to Medium: content delivery increasingly automates, but the course's function as gateway orientation to the major, situated within program requirements, keeps it instrumentally present. Diffusion research suggests firm-level and institutional adoption of AI teaching tools still lags raw capability, tempering how quickly this shift plays out in practice.

A decade out, AI is a capable, ever-present source for explaining surveying law, licensing structure, and professional practice concepts, and the case for a human-taught introductory lecture on these topics is substantially eroded on pure information-delivery grounds. Capability-trend research describing rapid task-horizon growth supports assuming AI explanatory competence continues improving through 2036. Still, the course's function as the first structured touchpoint for surveying majors, and its place in a program built around a technical, licensure-adjacent, accreditation-linked curriculum, persists absent a redesign of the degree sequence. The rating holds Medium, capped by that structural role rather than by task difficulty. The genuine uncertainty is whether programs restructure early orientation entirely around AI tools, not whether the underlying professional grounding this course targets remains institutionally anchored.
SUR 1000.d: This course addresses the basic legal, technical, and professional topics of land surveying. Students are introduced to the federal and state statutes and regulations governing professional practice. Technical subjects address daily professional practice of research, data collection, and data reduction.

r: Surveying I combines fieldwork with computation: students learn measurement theory, then collect and reduce angle, direction, distance, and elevation observations using total stations, electronic distance meters, tapes, and differential levels, and separately compute and adjust traverses and construction stakeout using CAD-interfaced data collectors. Task-exposure research places manual, real-time instrument operation and fieldwork among the least-exposed activity categories, while the traverse-computation and CAD portions are more exposed to current tools. This is the entry technical course and a hard prerequisite for nearly the entire upper-division surveying sequence, so its foundational-scaffolding role is direct rather than diffuse. At 24 months, the embodied field-measurement component and the course's gatekeeping role for downstream courses jointly hold the instrumental need firmly in place; software already assists the computational half, but that assistance does not remove the requirement to learn field measurement and its underlying theory.

By 2031, AI-integrated software will handle traverse computation, coordinate geometry, and stakeout calculations with little student intervention, substantially eroding the execution rationale for the computational half of the course. Field instrument operation—setting up a total station, running differential levels, recording usable field data—remains embodied, real-time, physically situated work that task-exposure frameworks continue to classify as low-exposure. Because this course gatekeeps essentially the entire subsequent surveying curriculum, its foundational role caps how far the rating can rise even as computation automates. The rating moves to Medium: AI absorbs the calculation workload, but the field-measurement competence and prerequisite function keep the course instrumentally necessary for any student continuing in the program. Diffusion of these tools into instructional field courses specifically, rather than professional practice, remains an open and slower-moving question.

A decade out, computation is thoroughly automated and even some field data capture may be assisted by robotic or AI-guided instruments, further narrowing the purely computational rationale for this course. But the underlying competence—understanding what a total station or level is measuring, recognizing blunders, and physically operating survey instrumentation—remains embodied work that current capability trends have not shown displacing hands-on field skill acquisition. The course's position as the load-bearing prerequisite for the entire surveying-technology sequence continues to cap the rating at Medium regardless of how far computational automation advances, since the program cannot restructure around AI without redesigning its foundational course architecture. The uncertainty concerns how much field practice time shrinks as automated tools assist data capture, not whether this foundational, partly embodied course remains instrumentally required for the major.
SUR 1510.d: This is an introductory course in elementary surveying. Students acquire a knowledge of the theory of measurements, methods of collecting and recording data, reduction of observations of angles, directions, distances and differences in elevation; the computation and adjustment of traverses; the use of data collectors and interfacing with CAD software; construction stakeout employing coordinate geometry and CAD output; and the methods of computing coordinate geometry and areas. Field work includes use of transits, total stations, electronic distance meters, surveyors' tapes, differential levels and data collectors.

r: Surveying II covers control surveying, state plane coordinate systems, construction surveying, legal and boundary surveying, and large-scale topographic mapping, using optical micrometers, electronic theodolites, precise levels, and electronic distance meters in field and lab settings that include astronomic azimuth observations, curve computation, earthwork surveys, and control networks. This is dense embodied instrument work paired with legal-boundary content where errors carry real property consequences—exactly the profile task-exposure research treats as low-exposure and the framework treats as high-verification-burden. As the prerequisite for surveying computations, boundary law, photogrammetry, and geodesy alike, it anchors nearly the full upper-division curriculum. At 24 months neither instrument-based control surveying nor the legal-boundary judgment components show meaningful AI displacement, and the course's structural centrality to everything that follows keeps the instrumental need for a human to take it fully intact.

By 2031, AI-assisted software may propose preliminary control networks or flag likely computation errors, and the curve, earthwork, and azimuth-computation elements will see meaningfully more automation support than today. But the operative work of this course is dual-locked: verification burden is high because boundary and control errors have real legal and construction consequences that a human surveyor must catch, and the field instrument work—running theodolites, precise levels, and distance meters to establish primary control—remains embodied, hands-on execution outside AI's competence. Because Surveying II is the load-bearing prerequisite for computations, boundary law, photogrammetry, and geodesy, its foundational role independently caps the rating. The rating holds Low: computational assistance grows, but neither the dampened verification-and-embodiment profile nor the prerequisite structure loosens enough by this horizon to shift the instrumental calculus.

A decade out, capability-trend research describing rapid growth in AI task competence suggests computational and even some field-assistive tools will be considerably more capable, but the course's core profile does not shift: control and boundary surveying combine embodied field measurement with adversarial, litigation-relevant legal-boundary judgment, both of which stay resistant on current evidence. This is the same combination—low embodiment, low verification-burden, and status as the prerequisite gateway to essentially the entire upper-division sequence—that holds the rating at Low across all three horizons rather than easing. The genuine uncertainty is how much AI-assisted instrumentation changes daily field practice for working surveyors by 2036, not whether the course's dual embodied-and-judgment core, and its structural position at the base of the curriculum, remain instrumentally necessary for a student entering the profession.
SUR 2520.d: This course is designed to cover the introduction to control surveying, state plane coordinate systems, construction surveying, legal and boundary surveying and large scale topographic mapping for engineering and architectural projects. The student is introduced to optical micrometer and electronic theodolites, precise levels, and electronic distancers. Laboratory assignments will cover astronomic azimuth observations, circular and parabolic curves, earthwork surveys, control surveying and topographic mapping.

r: Surveying Computations converts field observations into usable products—traverse computations, subdivision computations, and route-surveying computations—applying mathematics and surveying principles the student developed earlier in the sequence. This is desk-based, fully digital work with no fieldwork component, and it maps closely to well-defined mathematical procedures that current AI and COGO software already execute competently; observed-usage data confirms Computer & Mathematical tasks dominate current AI adoption. Even so, at 24 months the course remains structurally required: it is the prerequisite for survey data adjustment and analysis, and diffusion research shows firm- and program-level adoption of AI computation tools still lags what the technology can already do. Verification burden is moderate—computation errors that reach subdivision plats or route designs carry real cost—so the course's instrumental role in building the human capacity to set up and check these computations is not eroded at this horizon.

By 2031, AI tools will likely perform traverse, subdivision, and route computations with minimal manual setup, substantially weakening the case that a student must hand-execute these calculations to acquire the skill for practice. Productivity research on comparable well-defined technical tasks shows large speed gains from AI assistance, and this course's fully digital, no-fieldwork profile makes it a strong candidate for that kind of automation. What keeps the rating from rising further is the course's role as prerequisite substrate for survey data adjustment and its place in the accreditation-linked program sequence, which together cap the erosion at Medium. The rating rises from Low: raw computation increasingly automates, but the requirement to understand what the computations mean, in order to feed them into later coursework, keeps the course instrumentally present in the curriculum.

A decade out, computation of the kind this course teaches is close to fully automatable on capability grounds, and capability-trend research on rapid task-horizon growth supports assuming that trajectory continues. The instrumental case for manually performing traverse, subdivision, and route computations by hand is substantially eroded by this horizon. The rating nonetheless holds at Medium rather than falling further, because the course still functions as prerequisite scaffolding feeding directly into survey data adjustment and analysis, and the program's accreditation-linked structure has not shown signs of eliminating that sequencing. The genuine uncertainty is whether the course is restructured to teach computation verification and AI-output review rather than manual execution, not whether some version of this computational grounding remains structurally required for students continuing into upper-division surveying coursework.
SUR 2550.d: This is an introductory course on converting survey field observations/data into a form suitable to the end user. Students apply principles and precepts learned in courses of mathematics and surveying to surveying problems, develop analysis techniques, and perform those computations required for plane surveying problems encountered by the surveyor, land developer and civil engineer. Traverse computations, subdivision computations, route surveying computations, etc., are addressed.

r: This course teaches least-squares adjustment of survey networks—triangulation, traverses, trilateration, and vertical networks—using statistical condition and observation equations, entirely as desk-based statistical analysis with no fieldwork. Least-squares network adjustment is a mature, well-specified numerical procedure already heavily supported by commercial adjustment software, and observed-usage data confirms mathematical and computational tasks are the largest current category of AI use, so realized automatability is already high even at this horizon. Diffusion research indicates that adoption of AI-augmented statistical tooling in surveying curricula specifically still lags what the underlying capability supports, and the accreditation-linked program structure keeps the course in place regardless. Verification burden is moderate: adjustment outputs need review for blunders and mis-specified equations, work that still benefits from statistical training. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this statistical-adjustment competence directly is not eroded despite high raw task automatability.

By 2031, AI systems will very plausibly configure and run least-squares network adjustments largely unassisted, given that the underlying mathematics is exactly the kind of well-defined computational task where capability-trend research shows the fastest, most reliable gains. The instrumental rationale for manually deriving and solving observation equations weakens considerably. The rating rises to Medium rather than higher because the program's accreditation-linked structure keeps statistical-adjustment competence in the required sequence, and because a surveyor still needs the conceptual grounding to recognize when an AI-produced adjustment result is statistically sound versus masking a blunder or mis-modeled network. The course's role is narrower and more terminal than the foundational field courses, but it is not eliminated: understanding least-squares theory remains necessary to interpret and trust automated adjustment output.

A decade out, AI-driven adjustment of survey networks is plausibly routine, and the case for hand-deriving observation equations is largely gone on pure execution grounds. The rating holds at Medium rather than falling to Low or rising to High because two forces offset: task automatability is very high, but the accreditation-linked program structure keeps statistical survey theory in the required curriculum, and interpreting adjustment statistics to catch a subtly wrong AI-generated result still calls for the trained judgment this course builds. The uncertainty at this horizon is significant—whether adjustment theory is taught as a standalone computational exercise or folded into applied review-and-verification instruction is an open pedagogical question—but the underlying need for graduates to understand what a network adjustment is actually doing appears durable through 2036.
SUR 3100.d: This course provides a foundation in the basic principles of computational methods used to adjust and analyze survey observations employing statistical principles and least squares theory. The problems include adjustment of triangulation, traverses, trilateration, and vertical networks by condition and/or observation equations.

r: Astronomy for Surveyors teaches positional determination and azimuth/bearing calculation from astronomical observations, with students computing the azimuth of a line from actual survey observations. This is a specialized, largely computational course built on real observational data, with a moderate embodiment profile: the observation step has some field/real-time character even though the analytical work is desk-based. Task-exposure research treats structured mathematical computation as more exposed than physical, real-time activity, placing this course in between. Verification burden is moderate—an incorrectly computed azimuth propagates error into dependent survey work—so review by someone who understands the underlying spherical astronomy still matters. At 24 months, this specialized elective remains a required piece of the surveying-technology sequence at MSU Denver, and the instrumental need to learn astronomic positioning methods directly, rather than simply trusting an output, is not eroded.

By 2031, AI tools will competently walk through astronomic azimuth computation and could plausibly automate much of the calculation pipeline from observation data to final bearing, since this is exactly the kind of structured numerical procedure where capability-trend research shows fast improvement. The instrumental case for manually performing the computation weakens. What holds the rating from falling further is the program's accreditation-linked requirement structure, which keeps this specialized methods course in the sequence, and the residual value of understanding the underlying geometry well enough to sanity-check an automated result. The rating rises to Medium: the raw computation increasingly automates, but the course's place in the required technical curriculum and the interpretive competence it builds keep it instrumentally present, with real but bounded uncertainty about how the specific methods taught evolve.

A decade out, azimuth determination from astronomic or equivalent observations is very likely fully automatable end to end, and capability trends support assuming that continues improving through 2036. The course's specific technique may itself evolve or be supplemented by other positioning methods, which introduces genuine uncertainty about exactly what is taught by then. The rating holds Medium rather than falling to Low, anchored by the program's accreditation-linked curriculum requirements rather than by task difficulty, since the underlying subject matter's automatability is high. This is a case where institutional structure, not task resistance, is doing the work of keeping the course instrumentally present; if the accredited curriculum were restructured, this specific course would be among the more exposed candidates for consolidation.
SUR 3150.d: This is an introductory course on applying astronomical observations to surveying and mapping projects. Students acquire knowledge about positional determination by astronomical observations and determining the direction (azimuth, bearing) of lines on the earth's surface from astronomic observations. The students compute the azimuth of a line from actual survey observations.

r: Real Property Descriptions teaches students to write legal descriptions for deeds, easements, and rights-of-way, emphasizing precise structure and language to avoid ambiguity, plus interpreting descriptions when conflicts arise. This is fully desk-based legal drafting—text generation is exactly the task category task-exposure research finds strongly positively associated with AI exposure—so raw automatability is meaningfully higher than in the field courses. But verification burden is severe: an ambiguous or erroneous legal description creates real title disputes and litigation exposure, the adversarial, high-error-cost condition the jagged-frontier research associates with AI users being measurably less accurate outside their competence and prone to miscalibrated trust. Licensure-relevant content in this area functions as course-specific mandated subject matter analogous to other named licensing coursework. At 24 months, drafting assistance exists, but the instrumental need for a human trained in this precise discipline is not eroded.

By 2031, AI drafting tools will plausibly generate competent first-draft legal descriptions routinely, and productivity research on professional writing tasks shows AI assistance can cut drafting time substantially while changing quality profiles. That raises rather than lowers the verification stakes here: a fluent but subtly wrong legal description is a worse failure mode than a rough one, and the jagged-frontier findings on misplaced confidence outside an AI's reliable zone apply directly to boundary-adjacent legal drafting. The course-specific licensure relevance of this exact subject matter continues to anchor the rating. The rating holds Low: drafting execution becomes more AI-assisted, but the human competence to catch ambiguity, evaluate conflicting instrument language, and bear professional responsibility for the description is not something the institutional and liability structure allows to erode on this horizon.

A decade out, AI-generated legal descriptions may be a normal first pass in practice, and the raw drafting-execution rationale for teaching this by hand is substantially eroded—capability-trend research supports assuming fluent, well-formed draft language by then. The rating rises to Medium rather than staying Low because that erosion is real, but it is capped from reaching High by the mandated, licensure-relevant subject matter this course represents and by persistently high verification burden: property litigation is adversarial and non-obvious-failure by nature, exactly the domain where a human expert holding this exact knowledge remains structurally required. The uncertainty is substantial—how licensing bodies treat AI-assisted drafting competency by 2036 is unresolved—but the instrumental need for trained review of property-description language, as opposed to unsupervised generation, appears durable.
SUR 3220.d: This course addresses writing real property legal descriptions for deeds, easements, and rights-of-way. Emphasis is placed on the structure and order of the elements in the description and on avoiding the common mistakes of language, construction, and terminology in order to avoid ambiguities in the intent of the instrument. A study of the interpretation of the rules to deal with conflicts and ambiguities in instruments is presented.

r: Photogrammetry covers camera geometry, flight and project planning, supporting field surveys and field classification/targeting, photogrammetric plotters, and an introduction to digital-image scanning and GPS synchronization for engineering and mapping applications. The image-processing half of this content overlaps with computer-vision techniques where automated feature extraction and photogrammetric reconstruction are already commercially mature, giving this course a higher baseline task-exposure than purely field-based courses; but flight/project planning judgment and the field-survey support component retain a real embodied dimension. Verification burden is moderate: photogrammetric mapping products feed into engineering and legal work where errors matter but methodology includes established software checks. At 24 months, adoption of fully automated photogrammetric pipelines in an instructional setting is not complete, and the course's combined field-and-digital scope keeps the instrumental need for direct instruction intact.

By 2031, automated structure-from-motion and image-processing pipelines will very plausibly handle much of the technical photogrammetric workflow with limited manual intervention, and capability-trend research on fast task-horizon growth supports that trajectory for this computer-vision-adjacent domain. The execution rationale for teaching manual plotter and comparator technique weakens accordingly. The rating rises to Medium because the course's accreditation-linked program placement persists, and because flight planning, field-survey support, and quality judgment about automated outputs remain tasks requiring trained human oversight—an engineering and surveying application where a wrong automated reconstruction has real downstream cost for the resulting deliverable. The shift reflects execution automating faster here than in the purely field-based courses, offset by continued institutional requirement and residual verification and planning work that current AI capability does not yet fully absorb.

A decade out, photogrammetric and broader geospatial image-processing pipelines are plausibly near-fully automated on the technical execution side, consistent with rapid capability growth in computer-vision-adjacent domains. The rating holds Medium rather than rising to High because the accreditation-linked program structure keeps this specialized mapping course in the required sequence, and because someone must still plan the acquisition, verify georeferencing and coordinate integrity, and catch failures in an automated reconstruction before it feeds an engineering or legal deliverable. The genuine uncertainty is how much of this course's content is absorbed into a more general geospatial-data course as manual-technique portions become obsolete, not whether foundational photogrammetric literacy and human oversight competence remain instrumentally useful for surveying graduates working with mapping data by 2036.
SUR 3300.d: This course introduces the science of photogrammetry. The geometry of the photographic camera, vertical photography, aerial-mapping camera, flight planning, project planning, supporting field surveys and field classification and targeting are emphasized. Photogrammetric plotters and comparators are discussed. An introduction to digital-image scanning and GPS synchronization is presented. The application of photogrammetry to engineering and surveying mapping programs is discussed.

r: Boundary Law I covers proportionate measurement, senior/junior title rights, retracement of original surveys, deed-first/survey-first doctrine, case law, ranking conflicting evidence, and controlling monuments and corners—a course built on legal-judgment case analysis rather than fieldwork. Task-exposure research finds critical-thinking and judgment-heavy work strongly negatively associated with AI exposure, and boundary retracement is exactly this kind of adversarial, evidence-weighing discipline where a wrong professional conclusion produces real litigation. This subject area functions as course-specific, licensure-relevant mandated content, similar in kind to other named licensing coursework requirements. Verification burden is severe: boundary determinations carry legal liability, and jagged-frontier findings on miscalibrated AI confidence outside its reliable zone apply directly to this domain. At 24 months, the instrumental need for a human trained to rank evidence and apply boundary-law doctrine is fully intact.

By 2031, AI tools will likely summarize relevant case law and precedent competently, easing the research-gathering side of boundary analysis. But the professional act this course trains—weighing conflicting monument and deed evidence and reaching a defensible retracement conclusion under case law that varies by jurisdiction—remains the adversarial, high-stakes judgment task where jagged-frontier research shows AI users venturing outside a model's reliable zone become measurably less accurate while trusting the output more. The course-specific licensure relevance of boundary-law competency continues to anchor the rating, and this is exactly the profile the framework treats as a hard, course-specific mandate rather than a general credit-hour requirement. The rating holds Low: case-law retrieval automates, but the evidentiary judgment and licensure-tied competency this course builds are not displaced by that assistance on this horizon.

A decade out, AI legal-research and case-law synthesis tools are plausibly a standard input to boundary analysis, and the underlying language-processing tasks are well within projected capability growth. The rating rises modestly to Medium rather than staying Low because that research-support layer meaningfully changes how the analysis is prepared, even though it does not change who bears responsibility for the retracement judgment. It stays capped below High because the course-specific licensure relevance of boundary-law competency and the severe, adversarial verification burden of contested property determinations persist as structural constraints independent of AI capability. The genuine uncertainty is how licensing boards treat AI-assisted boundary analysis by 2036, not whether the trained human judgment this course builds remains instrumentally necessary to bear professional responsibility for the conclusion.
SUR 3540.d: This course introduces the concepts of boundary control and legal principles. Subjects addressed include proportionate measurement, rights in land, junior/senior title rights, retracement of original surveys, deed first/survey first, common and case law, ranking/prioritizing evidence, controlling monuments and corners, errors in legal descriptions and plats, and case studies.

r: Geodesy I introduces the theory of the earth's size and shape, the history of geodesy, classical procedures for determining latitude, longitude, elevation, and gravity field, and the underlying instrumentation and physical theory. This is a largely conceptual, lecture-oriented science course with minimal fieldwork as described, closer to an explanatory-content course than an applied-execution one. Task-exposure research finds explanatory, informational content increasingly within AI's competence, but observed diffusion of AI-based instruction specifically into accredited technical science courses still lags what the underlying models can do. Verification burden is moderate: geodetic theory underlies datum and coordinate-system correctness in later applied work, so getting the physical theory right matters. At 24 months, the instrumental need for structured instruction in geodetic theory as foundational science for the surveying-technology curriculum is not eroded despite the content's explanatory nature.

By 2031, AI systems will fluently explain geodetic theory, historical methods, and the physics underlying position and gravity determination, and task-exposure research supports treating this kind of conceptual, non-adversarial content as increasingly AI-deliverable. The instrumental case for dedicated classroom delivery of the historical and theoretical material weakens. The rating rises to Medium because the accreditation-linked program structure keeps geodetic science in the required technical curriculum regardless of how the material is delivered, and because the physical theory remains genuinely foundational to interpreting datum, coordinate-system, and gravity-model behavior in downstream geospatial and control-network work. The shift reflects content delivery automating while the underlying scientific-literacy requirement, tied to program structure and to foundational role rather than to task difficulty alone, persists across the horizon.

A decade out, AI explanation of geodetic theory and history is plausibly comprehensive and pedagogically effective, consistent with continued rapid growth in model capability described by capability-trend research on task-horizon doubling. The rating holds Medium rather than falling to Low or rising to High because the accreditation-linked program structure keeps this foundational science course in the surveying-technology sequence, while the scientific-literacy function it serves for later geospatial and control-network work retains genuine value that AI content delivery alone does not supply to the learner. The considerable uncertainty at this horizon concerns how introductory science instruction is restructured under ubiquitous AI tutoring generally, not whether foundational geodetic literacy remains instrumentally useful for graduates who must interpret coordinate systems and datums throughout their careers.
SUR 3700.d: This is an introduction into the science of geodesy. The course presents an overview into the theory of surveying in which the size and shape of the earth must be addressed. The history of geodesy and the classical survey procedures to determine latitude, longitude, elevation, and the earth's gravity field are presented. The underlying theory of instrumentation and the application of physical theory are discussed.

r: This course teaches retracement of Public Land Survey System boundaries: interpreting General Land Office field notes and original plats, distinguishing original surveys from resurveys, and resolving mineral, riparian, and bona-fide-rights questions under the Manual of Surveying for the Public Lands. These interpretive tasks map to O*NET's information-interpretation and standards-compliance activities, weighing historical monument evidence against statute and precedent. Task-exposure research finds that science and critical-thinking-heavy work is negatively associated with exposure, a pattern that fits contested boundary retracement, where AI can retrieve and summarize archival records but cannot adjudicate ambiguous evidentiary conflicts. Colorado's licensing board expects surveyors to master PLSS doctrine directly, a course-specific mandate independent of any general-studies designation. Verification burden is severe, since an erroneous boundary call carries litigation exposure. At 24 months the instrumental need to master this material is essentially unchanged, execution assistance aside.

By 2031, AI tools will fluently retrieve General Land Office records, draft preliminary retracement narratives, and flag plat inconsistencies, eroding some research-heavy preparation work this course covers. But the deterministic-rule dampener holds because boundary adjudication remains a licensure-gated, board-approved curricular requirement with genuinely high verification burden: courts and clients still need a certified professional accountable for the legal judgment behind a boundary call, not merely a plausible-sounding narrative. Task-exposure research's negative association between critical-thinking demands and AI exposure continues to describe this content reasonably well. The instrumental case shifts from "AI cannot do this" toward "AI drafts, the licensed surveyor certifies and defends," which keeps the course necessary but changes its emphasis toward judgment and evidentiary reasoning rather than manual record retrieval. Confidence in this trajectory is moderate; licensure requirements evolve slowly, but drafting-tool adoption could outpace this estimate.

A decade out, AI systems will likely handle most PLSS document synthesis and first-draft boundary narratives competently, per the fast capability trend observed in task-time-horizon research. Diffusion research suggests adoption still lags capability unevenly across small survey firms, and the institutional brake persists: a board-approved, licensure-specific curriculum covering PLSS doctrine is unlikely to disappear absent regulatory change, since land-boundary certification carries legal liability that clients and courts will continue to require a human license-holder to bear. The rating rises to Medium rather than higher, reflecting real erosion of manual research tasks alongside a durable licensure-anchored core. This is a genuine hedge: how much of PLSS coursework remains instrumentally necessary versus AI-assisted with human sign-off a decade out depends on regulatory and professional-liability decisions not yet visible from current evidence.
SUR 3800.d: This course describes the survey procedures contained in the current Manual of Surveying for the Public Lands of the United States (1973). The history, design, and planning of the rectangular survey system, original surveys, resurveys, independent and dependent surveys, protection of bona-fide rights, mineral surveys, special surveys, and riparian rights are addressed. The importance of the official plats and field notes are presented.

r: This course trains students to translate engineering and architectural plans into field construction surveys and post-construction payment mapping, covering measurement tolerances, terrestrial photography and control, deformation monitoring, and hazardous-site safety. These are embodied, real-time tasks -- setting instruments, monitoring structures under construction, working in hazardous environments -- mapped to O*NET's equipment-inspection and process-monitoring activities. Task-exposure research classifies manual and physical work as low-exposure, and that classification fits fieldwork directly. AI can assist with deformation-data analysis and tolerance calculations, but the on-site measurement and safety judgment this course teaches is not something a model can substitute for at present. Verification burden is real too: construction payment and structural-safety consequences of a bad measurement are costly, keeping expert oversight load-bearing. At 24 months the instrumental need for hands-on field-measurement training is essentially undiminished.

By 2031, AI-assisted deformation analysis, tolerance-checking software, and automated total-station data processing will likely handle more of the calculation and documentation load this course currently teaches by hand, per the fast capability trend in automated reasoning tasks. But the physical core -- setting control on an active construction site, taking terrestrial-photography measurements, working safely around hazardous materials -- stays embodied work that instrument automation assists rather than replaces, so the dampener from low embodiment and moderate verification burden continues to apply. The rating rises modestly toward Medium as data-processing execution automates around a still-physical fieldwork core, consistent with the accreditation-linked program mandate that keeps the subject matter required even as specific tasks shift. This is a moderate-confidence projection: instrumentation automation, such as robotic total stations and UAS photogrammetry, could compress the field-labor share faster than assumed.

A decade out, construction-site measurement technology will likely be substantially more autonomous -- semi-robotic instruments, drone-based deformation monitoring -- following the compute and capability trends observed broadly. Yet someone must still be physically present to set control, verify readings against site conditions, and hold responsibility when tolerances or safety are at stake, and the program's accreditation-linked coursework mandate is not expected to lapse. The rating holds at Medium: substantial automation of data reduction and reporting coexists with a durable, if narrower, requirement for embodied field competence and construction-site safety judgment. The genuine uncertainty is how much of the fieldwork itself becomes remote-supervised or robot-assisted by 2036 -- current diffusion evidence shows real AI adoption remains uneven across firms, so field practice may lag capability substantially.
SUR 4500.d: This course introduces the student to the methods of translating engineering and architectural plans into field surveys for construction work and post-construction mapping for payments. The topics include engineering measurement tolerances, vertical and horizontal differential tolerances, terrestrial photography and control, deformation studies and analysis, safety and hazardous waste environment.

r: This course teaches the mathematics of conformal map projections (Lambert conformal conic, Mercator, transverse Mercator, oblique Mercator, stereographic, Albers equal area), projection-system design, and transformation between plane coordinates and geodetic positions -- fully digital, computational tasks mapped to O*NET's data-analysis and information-processing activities. Observed-usage data shows Computer & Mathematical work is already the largest AI-usage category, and this course's content -- closed-form coordinate transformation, projection parameter selection -- sits squarely inside that category. Verification burden is moderate: transformed coordinates can be checked against known control, unlike open-ended legal judgment. Even so, the senior-standing prerequisite and the program's accreditation-linked structure anchor the course in the required curriculum today. At 24 months the instrumental case is already partly eroded for routine computation, though the underlying theory the course builds is still taught, not yet outsourced wholesale.

By 2031, AI and GIS/CAD tooling will very likely perform routine projection transformations and parameter selection with little friction, extending the pattern task-exposure research already identifies: programming and quantitative computation are strongly positively associated with AI exposure, unlike critical-thinking-heavy legal work. With no embodiment or severe-verification dampener protecting this content -- the math is checkable and largely digital -- the base rating from rising task automatability climbs to Medium, held there only by the program's accreditation-linked mandate for this coursework rather than by any inherent resistance to automation. The instrumental case shifts toward understanding what the software computes well enough to catch a bad datum or misapplied projection, rather than performing transformations by hand. Confidence is moderate: how much conceptual grounding survives once transformation tools are ubiquitous is a genuinely open curricular question.

A decade out, this material sits close to the discipline's most AI-exposed core: closed-form geodetic and cartographic mathematics that fast capability trends and already-strong current AI performance on quantitative tasks make highly automatable. GDPval-style evidence on real deliverable performance suggests models are approaching, though not yet matching, expert-level output on structured technical work like this. The rating holds at Medium rather than High only because the accreditation-linked program requirement keeps the topic in the required curriculum regardless of how fully AI performs the underlying computation. The genuine hedge here is curricular, not technical: whether programs continue teaching hand computation of projections once tooling is universal, or restructure the course around verification and projection-system judgment, is a pedagogical choice not yet resolved by any evidence in hand.
SUR 4510.d: This is an in-depth course addressing the popular conformal map projections employed in surveying and mapping programs. The theories for the Lambert conformal conic, Mercator, transverse Mercator, oblique Mercator and stereographic, and Albers equal area projections are presented. Designing the projection system, transformation between plane coordinates and geodetic positions and the conversion of survey data to map projection data are emphasized. The use of local conformal map projections will be presented. Sustainable Systems Engineering
